Candidates for circumcision after washing do not return to warm themselves at their father's (but go straightway to the place of the ceremony to show their courage). In things that must be it is good to be resolute.
The food that is in the mouth is not yet in the belly. Do not cry herrings till they are in the net.
When the food is cooked there is no need to wait before eating it.
What is in Masai is not in Kikuyu. There is many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip.

The pit allows the grass to fall in.

The proverb alludes to the pits the Kikuyu used to dig for trapping wild animals. These pits were covered with sticks over which, as well as over the borders, they put a layer of grass. Since this grass often fell in the pit through the spaces between the sticks, so they say that often one falls into the pit dug by himself.

senses.definition:
When ‘ithare’ is uprooted ‘mūgumo’ grows in its place.

‘Ithare’ is a kind of cane growing on the river banks. The Kikuyu say it is of no use. ‘Mūgumo’ is a kind of fig tree (Ficus Hochstetteri) which does not grow except leaning on another tree or twisting around it like a creeper. This is why they think that the ‘mūgumo’ is worse than the ‘ithare’.

Shyness has no sucking. It means that if a calf is shy it will be afraid to approach its mother and consequently will get no milk.

Whom we love best, them we want to be happy.

The song of a stranger-woman is answered after she has gone. The proverb is metaphorically used to mean that foreigners, especially women, are not to be trusted too much. Eat a peck of salt with a man before you trust him.
It is bad to stay at home. He that stays in the valley shall never get over the hill.
He who does not know, knows after being told. A man forewarned is forearmed.
He who does not know the road delays also one that knows it. Who goes with a fool becomes a fool.

The rich man cannot be prevented from cultivating the 'iganjo' he wants. 'Iganjo' is the place upon which a hut had been built. Since the flocks live in the owner's hut, the floor of the hut becomes fertilized. The proverb refers to the fact that if a rich man has left a piece of his land to a poor man on which to build his hut, very often he wants it back as soon as the soil under the hut has been enriched by the droppings of the animals. Might is right.
Rich people sometimes eat bad food. All is not gold that glitters.
Thieves conceal themselves in the night not in the day. The night is a cloak for sinners.
To get the warmth of fire one must stir the embers. No gains without pains.
The fear (of toil) keeps your house poor. Idleness is the key of beggary.
If you help yourself you will be helped. God helps those who help themselves.

headword: Gūtema na kanua ti gūtema na rūhiū

senses.definition: Cutting by the tongue is different from cutting by the knife. Slander is not mortal stabbing. Hard words break no bones.

A man changing his abode is like a woman marrying. As a woman, on marrying, adopts the customs of the family she enters, so a man going to live in a strange country, must accept its customs. When in Rome do as Rome does.

headword: Gūthekererwo ni andũ ti kūririrwo ni hiti

senses.definition: To be laughed at by men is not to be wept by hyenas. Better to be laughed at than to die.
To be laughed at is not to be pitied. One starting any enterprise ought not to fear what others say of him. Do well and dread no shame.
If anybody makes you laugh, it is not always because he loves you. Eat a peck of salt with a man before you trust him.

Nobody entering a hut pays for the heat he will enjoy in it. Only the owner of the hut had the drudgery of carrying home the firewood: the visitor does not know the cost of the fire he is enjoying. Metaphorically the proverb is used to say that he who enters a house cannot realise the troubles of the occupants.

examples.text: Nobody entering a hut pays for the heat he will enjoy in it. Only the owner of the hut had the drudgery of carrying home the firewood: the visitor does not know the cost of the fire he is enjoying. Metaphorically the proverb is used to say that he who enters a house cannot realise the troubles of the occupants.

notes: None knows the weight of another’s burden.

headword: Gũtirĩ mündũ ũĩ haria egũthĩĩ no haria ekuuma

senses.definition: Nobody knows where he goes, but only whence he comes. No one can see into the future.

examples.text: Nobody knows where he goes, but only whence he comes. No one can see into the future.

headword: Gũtirĩ mündũ wendaga gũtũngana na nyoni njũru

senses.definition: Nobody wants to meet an ill-omened bird. To the Kikuyu many birds foreshadow calamity. The cry of the owl forebodes mishap. If the owl cries, perched on the top of a hut, the oldest man in that village will die very soon. If someone, about to make a journey, hears the cry of any bird of ill-omen, he must not start on any account. Nobody seeks his own ruin.

examples.text: Nobody wants to meet an ill-omened bird. To the Kikuyu many birds foreshadow calamity. The cry of the owl forebodes mishap. If the owl cries, perched on the top of a hut, the oldest man in that village will die very soon. If someone, about to make a journey, hears the cry of any bird of ill-omen, he must not start on any account. Nobody seeks his own ruin.

senses.definition: There is no man that cannot become an orphan. No flying from fate.

examples.text: There is no man that cannot become an orphan. No flying from fate.

headword: Gũtirĩ mündũ wonaga wega wake, no kuonwo wonagwo

senses.definition: Nobody can see his own goodness: it can be seen only by others.

examples.text: Nobody can see his own goodness: it can be seen only by others.

senses.definition: There is no pleasure (however little it may be) that does not cause one’s cheeks to tremble. The Kikuyu consider the cheek trembling an expression of joy. A little pleasure is nevertheless a pleasure.

examples.text: There is no pleasure (however little it may be) that does not cause one’s cheeks to tremble. The Kikuyu consider the cheek trembling an expression of joy. A little pleasure is nevertheless a pleasure.

senses.definition: No day dawns like another. Every day brings a new light.

examples.text: No day dawns like another. Every day brings a new light.

senses.definition: Nobody is born wise.

examples.text: Nobody is born wise.

senses.definition: Nobody returns where he got his finger bitten.

examples.text: Nobody returns where he got his finger bitten.

headword: Gütiri ūkagia ūtūmī atari na haria akuratha

senses.definition: Once bitten twice shy.

examples.text: Once bitten twice shy.

senses.definition: There is a reason for everything.

examples.text: There is a reason for everything.

senses.definition: Nobody walks with another man's gait.

examples.text: Nobody walks with another man's gait.

headword: Gütiri ūragio ni ūtonga no ūkia

senses.definition: There is nothing without a cause.

examples.text: There is nothing without a cause.

senses.definition: All things have a beginning.

examples.text: All things have a beginning.

senses.definition: Nobody grumbles at being rich, all at being poor.

examples.text: Nobody grumbles at being rich, all at being poor.

headword: Gütiri ūru ūtūraga, no wega ūtūraga

senses.definition: There is no mischance you are guaranteed against.

examples.text: There is no mischance you are guaranteed against.

senses.definition: There is no bow without its meat.

examples.text: There is no bow without its meat.

senses.definition: There is no name which cannot distinguish a child.

examples.text: There is no name which cannot distinguish a child.

senses.definition: A little idleness causes the ruin of the beehive.

examples.text: The Kikuyu hang beehives on the branches of the forest trees, and it is their custom to visit them often to make sure that they are all right. For it might happen that if out of idleness one did not see them regularly, one would ultimately find the branch broken, the beehive fallen and the contents spoilt.

senses.definition: Many people together lift up the ‘ndĩrĩ’.

examples.text: 'Ndĩrĩ’ is a heavy wooden mortar in which the Kikuyu women, when brewing beer, crush the sugar-cane. Many hands make light work.

senses.definition: Take an oath only for the hand you slept on.

examples.text: Swear only to that which you know to be true.

senses.definition: The whetstone in a village does not blunt the knife.

examples.text: Every potter praises his own pots.

senses.definition: The mouth who ate the seeds asks, ‘Now what shall I plant?’. He sups ill who eats up all at dinner.

examples.text: The mouth who ate the seeds asks, ‘Now what shall I plant?’. He sups ill who eats up all at dinner.

senses.definition: Another’s mouth cannot take the oath for you.

examples.text: Every bird must hatch its own eggs.

senses.definition: The mouth is a chink.

examples.text: From the mouth come many futilities.

senses.definition: The mouth sells the head.

examples.text: The tongue talks at the head’s cost.

senses.definition:
You spoke (against yourself) with your own mouth.
It means that one can sometimes condemn oneself in defending oneself.

A small red snuff-box is a welcome.
The proverb refers to the Kikuyu custom of giving a pinch of snuff to their friends when they meet.

The little bird that flaps its wings too much will spoil them.
One must crawl before one can walk.

'Kanywanjui' scratches its thigh.
'Kanywanjui' is a species of tiny blue bird with a long bill, which sucks nectar from flowers. The proverb means that such birds, although very small, can do everything for their own needs, and do not require others’ help to have their legs scratched.
Every man something can.

He who is stricken knows how to defend himself.
Scalded cats fear even cold water.

It is not the owner, trampling his own field, that spoils it (but the others).
The proverb has arisen from the fact that many people if they have a bad harvest, say that it is the fault of other people who walked across their plantations.
Nobody calls himself a rogue.

A person will change his mind on something if left to sleep over it.
Never leave till tomorrow what you can do today.
The fool hides himself under the eaves of the hut and thinks nobody will see him. It refers to foolish people who invent silly excuses to conceal their faults.

examples.text: The fool hides himself under the eaves of the hut and thinks nobody will see him.
examples.translation: The fool hides himself under the eaves of the hut and thinks nobody will see him.

senses.definition: He who feigns to be stupid is more stupid than the stupid-born. None so deaf as those who won't hear.

examples.text: He who feigns to be stupid is more stupid than the stupid-born. None so deaf as those who won't hear.
examples.translation: He who feigns to be stupid is more stupid than the stupid-born. None so deaf as those who won't hear.

senses.definition: A fool can even suck the mother after she is dead.

examples.text: A fool can even suck the mother after she is dead.
examples.translation: A fool can even suck the mother after she is dead.

senses.definition: A fool is like a beehive. The proverb means that he is a fool who does not look after his own interest, like the beehive which allows itself to be emptied.

examples.text: A fool is like a beehive. The proverb means that he is a fool who does not look after his own interest, like the beehive which allows itself to be emptied.
examples.translation: A fool is like a beehive. The proverb means that he is a fool who does not look after his own interest, like the beehive which allows itself to be emptied.

senses.definition: To force a woman to do something she doesn't like is like forcing a blunt shaving-knife to shave.

examples.text: To force a woman to do something she doesn't like is like forcing a blunt shaving-knife to shave.
examples.translation: To force a woman to do something she doesn't like is like forcing a blunt shaving-knife to shave.

senses.definition: He who has a sore does not feel sick on account of it. We are blind to our own faults.

examples.text: He who has a sore does not feel sick on account of it. We are blind to our own faults.
examples.translation: He who has a sore does not feel sick on account of it. We are blind to our own faults.

senses.definition: All the species of the chameleon family shall always have a protruding backbone. That that comes of cat will catch mice.

examples.text: All the species of the chameleon family shall always have a protruding backbone. That that comes of cat will catch mice.
examples.translation: All the species of the chameleon family shall always have a protruding backbone. That that comes of cat will catch mice.

senses.definition: Do not force a big thread into a bead with a small hole. Grasp all, lose all.

examples.text: Do not force a big thread into a bead with a small hole. Grasp all, lose all.
examples.translation: Do not force a big thread into a bead with a small hole. Grasp all, lose all.

senses.definition: A wasted thing cannot be eaten. Wilful waste makes woeful want.

examples.text: A wasted thing cannot be eaten. Wilful waste makes woeful want.
examples.translation: A wasted thing cannot be eaten. Wilful waste makes woeful want.

senses.definition: The goat and the child are not insulted (because they cannot defend themselves).

examples.text: The goat and the child are not insulted (because they cannot defend themselves).

senses.definition:
One can always find the goat to pay the penalty for having defecated in another's house.
According to Kikuyu customs he who defecates in another's house is liable to be fined a goat. The proverb means that he who incurred such penalty will contrive to find the means to pay it.
Necessity sharpens industry.

examples.text:

senses.definition:
A chattering goat does not keep its tongue.
The word 'goat' is here used instead of 'people'.
A fool may ask more questions in an hour than a wise man can answer in seven years.

examples.text:
A chattering goat does not keep its tongue.
The word 'goat' is here used instead of 'people'.
A fool may ask more questions in an hour than a wise man can answer in seven years.

senses.definition:
The best part of another's goat is the car.
The proverb means that a stranger coming in when a slaughtered goat is distributed, must not expect to be given a choice morsel, but rather an inferior part like an ear. Metaphorically the proverb means that a prudent person keeps for himself and his family the best parts of anything instead of giving them away to his visitors and friends.
Charity begins at home.

examples.text:
The best part of another's goat is the car.

Metaphorically the proverb means that a prudent person keeps for himself and his family the best parts of anything instead of giving them away to his visitors and friends.
Charity begins at home.

senses.definition:
The goat which eats ashes does not hide its habit.
The Kikuyu live under the same roof as their animals.
So if any goat forms the habit of leaving its place and coming to lick ashes at the fire, it will soon be discovered.
In the same manner the vices of the wicked will soon be known.

senses.definition: An old goat does not sneeze without cause.

examples.text: The proverb means that old folks speak the truth and do not speak without a reason.
examples.translation: The proverb means that old folks speak the truth and do not speak without a reason.

examples.text: Old dogs bark not for nothing.
examples.translation: Old dogs bark not for nothing.

senses.definition: Goats are not bananas (which are given for nothing). There are no gains without pains.

examples.text: There are no gains without pains.
examples.translation: There are no gains without pains.

headword: Mbũri ya ngĩa yaringĩrĩra no ũguo bata ũringagĩrĩra

senses.definition: When the poor man's goat is about to kid, then the need drops also. The proverb means that if a man rejoices because his goat is going to kid and so increase his property, a sudden need might force him to sell his goat. Count not your chickens before they be hatched.

examples.text: Count not your chickens before they be hatched.
examples.translation: Count not your chickens before they be hatched.

headword: Mbu ya arũme ifikagio ni athamaki

senses.definition: Men's alarm-shouts are answered by the elders. The proverb means that if the alarm is shouted only by women one can make light of it; but if the alarm is cried by men there exists a real danger. Metaphorically the proverb means that women cannot claim any right of discussing or giving evidence in a court. Let women spin and not preach.

examples.text: Let women spin and not preach.
examples.translation: Let women spin and not preach.

senses.definition: The bell needs its tongue. In this proverb the word 'bell' means 'woman', and 'tongue' means 'man'. Wives must be had, be they good or bad.

examples.text: Wives must be had, be they good or bad.
examples.translation: Wives must be had, be they good or bad.

headword: Mburungo nyinyi ũĩ mũthiomeri ũrugite nene itari mũthiomeri

senses.definition: A trifle well presented becomes more precious than a thing of great value badly presented. It is not the value of a gift that matters but the intentions of the giver.

examples.text: It is not the value of a gift that matters but the intentions of the giver.
examples.translation: It is not the value of a gift that matters but the intentions of the giver.

senses.definition: A distant water does not quench one's thirst.
Be not too proud lest you ruin yourself.

The 'miano' cannot be confused, but the mouth can. 'Miano' are the small gourds used by witch-doctors to contain the divining stones. The proverb means that the divining stones cannot fail to tell the truth, though it may happen that the witch-doctor does not tell it. God cures and the doctor takes the fee.
The words are the odour of the heart. The tongue ever turns to the aching tooth.
Two hides are not laid out at the same time. One cannot be in two places at once.

headword: Migũire ya ngũ na ya migogo ti imwe

senses.definition: The fall of branches and that of big trees are not the same.
Speaking in a whisper is followed by hiding (in order to steal). The proverb means that people who whisper are probably arranging something evil. Beware of a silent dog and still water.

headword: Mitheko ĩtarĩ githimi yumaga kanua-ini ka irimũ

senses.definition: Laugh without measure comes out of fools' mouths. The laughter of fools.
One's pocket is not a repository (in which all people can put their hands). Pocket means in this case home affairs. Scald not your lips in another man's pottage.
The hand has not to be put into another's pocket. Scald not your lips in another man's pottage.
He who is in necessity does not feel ashamed (to ask for help).
A cob of maize can knock down a giant. A small leak will sink a great ship.
It is he who travels that finds the tusk. God helps those who help themselves.

Yaws is caught through friendship. The proverb means that just as the disease is contracted by contact with infected people, so bad habits are acquired by consorting with bad people. Who keeps company with a wolf will learn to howl.
He who looks for another must find him. He who will seek may find.
He who walks with a mangy man becomes mangy. He who keeps company with a wolf will learn to howl.
Parents are merciful.

headword: Mūciari ndairagio ngoro ni kimira kia mwana wake

senses.definition: Parents do not feel sick when wiping the mucus from their child's nose.
Parents do not take away the earth that covers the root of the sugar cane.

headword: Mũgiri rwa kũnyitūra agirire rwa kũnyitia

senses.definition: One can cause the illness which he wanted to cure. The cure may be worse than the disease.
He who irritates will be scratched. Let sleeping dogs lie.
One trunk does not close a river. One flower makes no garland.
The she-sheep can break the cooking pot, and still she has no horn. Cooking pot means here an affair of great importance. The meaning of the proverb is that a fool can spoil wise people's affairs.
A field begins to become a wilderness from a side; i.e. from a small place. A little neglect may breed a great mischief.

headword: Mũgũnda wa mwere ũmenyagwo na ngetho

senses.definition: One knows a field of millet from its crop. The tree is known by its fruits.
Another's field is not praised. The proverb refers to the fact that the Kikuyu when they are drunk imagine themselves very rich, and so become proud of others' riches.
The man who buys something at a place near by is like the man who is given something. That is little esteemed that costs little.

headword: Mũgũi ũtarĩ wa awa ni ũkündembũrĩra thiaka

senses.definition: The arrow which is not my father's, pierces my quiver. Ill gotten goods seldom prosper.
He who pays another with his own things, does not bleed. The proverb means that one spends his money willingly when he needs help.
He who stands close to his things does not lose them. The master's eye makes the horse fat.
The messenger of peace has no two knives (presents). Messengers should neither be beheaded nor hanged.
He who plants is not he who eats. Man proposes, God disposes.
The one with diarrhoea must look for a bush. Let him that is cold blow the coal.
He who is spoken to at both ears does not understand. Too much consulting confounds.
A liar does not laugh (for if a liar laughs when he tells a lie he is not believed).

headword: Mūhenia ago oigaga mūrimū ūri gūthira

senses.definition: He who would deceive the witch-doctors says that his illness is finished. Hide nothing from thy minister, physician and lawyer.
The deceived has many more days than the deceiver. Liars have short wings.
The deceived is not so cunning as the deceiver.
He who receives must not measure. Do not look a gift horse in the mouth.
The child is not given away without a price.

examples.text: The proverb is used especially by a father to the young man wanting to marry his daughter. It must be borne in mind that the Kikuyu girl is not given to her husband, but she is bought by him.
examples.translation: No gains without pains.

senses.definition: The son is not beaten when the father is near.
The son need not ask his father for a piece of meat (for a parent spontaneously gives his children the best food).
A child who likes work does not lack one to wash him, i.e. to take care of him.
God tempers the wind to the thorn lamb.

headword: Mwana wa ndigwa niwe ũi kwiera

senses.definition: The baby that has some one to care for it does not dirty itself.

headword: Mwana wa ngari akunyaga ka nyina

senses.definition: Young and old age complete each other.

headword: Mwana wa ngori ndekagira njugiri kũgũrũ

senses.definition: The orphan boy wears no rattles on his feet.

headword: Mwana wa rwendo ariaga nyina na itie

senses.definition: The Kikuyu used to wear rattles on their feet when dancing.
A boy is not sent to collect the honey (for he does not know how to collect it). Every man does his own business best.

What have you that we have not? Nothing but ‘thũmbĩ’ and wind. ‘Thũmbĩ’ is the piece of cloth or leather used to fasten ostrich and other birds’ feathers around the head. The proverb means, ‘There is no news’.

headword: Mwathwo ni nda arũgĩte mwathwo ni ithe

senses.definition: Being ruled by one’s stomach is better than being ruled by one’s father.
Good people are sucked.
He that wants to become rich must till the earth.
He who wants papyrus-ashes burns papyrus. Previous to the advent of Europeans, the Kikuyu used papyrus-ashes, which are supposed to be rich in sodium, for cooking purposes.

headword: Mwendi mũhiriga ũtuikane etagia rũrĩmĩ na mbere ndarũriaga

senses.definition: He who wants to cause disagreement within the clan asks for the tongue (of the slaughtered goat) which he was not wont to eat before. The tongue of the goat is a choice morsel which belongs by right to the head of the family or clan. The proverb means that he who wants a pretext for quarrelling, asks for something which he cannot be given.
He who seeks evil finds it.
He who wants beauty does not complain (if it costs him some pain). No gains without pains.
He who sells buys. To buy and to sell are both business.
He who is loved receives no refusal.
The barber who shaves badly does not know any other (better) way of shaving. The first degree of folly is to think himself wise, the second is to tell others so, the third is to despise all counsel.
The good millet is known at the harvest time. A tree is known by its fruit.
He who waits gets the best food, i.e. the biggest potato, the sweetest maize, etc. and can eat better cooked food.
He who wants to dig out a potato does not use a blunt pole. The proverb means that he who wants to accomplish something, uses just those means that ensure success.

The frog that compared itself to the ox lost its buttocks. There is a fable, that a frog seeing what big buttocks the ox had, thought it could grow as big by swelling. But it burst and so lost buttocks and life. All covet, all lose.

The beard-pincers are not inherited.
It must be remembered that the Kikuyu do not shave but
pull out the beard with pincers forged by native blacksmiths
. The proverb means that there are some things
which are so personal that the father does not bequeath
them to his son; he has to get his own.

The fame is never up to its owner's merit,
He that doth good for praise only, merieth but a puff of wind.
To good clothes no ornament is added.

headword: Ngwa mbere ti noru ta ngwa thutha

senses.definition: The first fall is not as bad as the second fall.
Every man's tale is good till another's be told.

headword: Ngware ikirara mutti iguru ndiatigiro kuri kwega

senses.definition:
Potatoes are not praised when they are dug out (but when
they are eaten).
The proof of the pudding is in the eating.

The francolin is not killed in the courtyard.
According to Kikuyu superstition to kill a francolin found
on one's courtyard brings in misfortune. If anybody has
done it, he must slaughter a goat to propitiate the spirits.
There is a measure in all things.

headword: Ngware nyinyi iri na mukuririe wayo

senses.definition:
The little francolin has its way of scratching.
Every man his way.
A hero dies with the other.

examples.text: The proverb refers to the days of war before the advent of Europeans, when warriors went together to plunder and were bound to win or to die together.

senses.definition: One strong man only cannot close the ford of a river.
A strong man is not overpowered by his task.
A powerful man does not dominate two seasons.
A strong man is the ornament of his age-group.
Strength does not dwell in the calves of the legs.

examples.text: The proverb means that one's strength does not dwell in one's appearance, but rather in mind and virtue.

headword: Njau irĩ ndoge nyina ni ndoge

senses.definition: If the calf has been poisoned, also its mother has been (For they ordinarily eat the same food).

examples.text: Like father, like son.

senses.definition: He who waits does not arrive.

examples.text: Never leave that till tomorrow which you can do today.

senses.definition: 'Do to me and do to me' have no bitterness.

examples.text: The proverb means that a person cannot complain on receiving from others the same kind of treatment as he had given to them.

senses.definition: The road never says to the traveller, 'Take a rest'.

examples.text: The road never says to the traveller, 'Take a rest'.

senses.definition: A short way is only the way to bed.

examples.text: A short way is only the way to bed.

senses.definition: The elephant is not overpowered by its tusks.

examples.text: The elephant is not overpowered by its tusks.

senses.definition: The beer is a thing that unites (the tongue).

examples.text: The beer is a thing that unites (the tongue).

senses.definition: A bird that picks food with the beak does not collect food for another bird.

examples.text: A bird that picks food with the beak does not collect food for another bird.

senses.definition: The bee has not got two stings.

examples.text: The bee has not got two stings.

senses.definition: A strong man's club is tested by foreigners.

examples.text: A strong man's club is tested by foreigners.

senses.definition: Slander is worse than a river in flood.

examples.text: Slander is worse than a river in flood.

senses.definition: The little house discusses its affairs by night (because they are not worth discussion by day with waste of time).

examples.text: The little house discusses its affairs by night (because they are not worth discussion by day with waste of time).

headword: Nyũmba nyinyi yoragana yathama, yoragwo yathama

senses.definition: If a member of a small family is killed or kills another, the family moves (since it may be unable to defend itself).

examples.text: If a member of a small family is killed or kills another, the family moves (since it may be unable to defend itself).

senses.definition: The pot cooks the food and does not eat it. Bees that make honey, do not taste it.

examples.text: The pot cooks the food and does not eat it. Bees that make honey, do not taste it.

senses.definition: A rotten gourd seed does not germinate. Immoral people seldom get offspring.

examples.text: A rotten gourd seed does not germinate. Immoral people seldom get offspring.

senses.definition: The pot in which fat is stored does not break (for it is well fed).

examples.text: The pot in which fat is stored does not break (for it is well fed).

senses.definition: The cooking pot from which many people await their food, does not lack him who takes it from the fire. In like way, the problem in which many people are interested, will have one able to solve it.

examples.text: The cooking pot from which many people await their food, does not lack him who takes it from the fire. In like way, the problem in which many people are interested, will have one able to solve it.

senses.definition: Every man makes up his own bed. Every bird must hatch its own eggs.

examples.text: Every man makes up his own bed. Every bird must hatch its own eggs.

headword: O mũndũ ahuragia mwaki na mwihirito wake

senses.definition: Every man scratches in his fire and in his ‘mwihirito’. ‘Mwihirito’ is the space between any two of the three stones of the Kikuyu hearth. Everyone should sweep before his own door.

examples.text: Every man scratches in his fire and in his ‘mwihirito’. ‘Mwihirito’ is the space between any two of the three stones of the Kikuyu hearth. Everyone should sweep before his own door.

senses.definition: A short hide is of no value.

examples.text: A short hide is of no value.

senses.definition:
The owner of the goat does not give away its hide.

The proverb refers to the fact that the skin of a slaughtered goat belongs by right to the animal's owner, who does not allow anybody else to have it for nothing.

Metaphorically it means that nobody gives his life but for a cause worthy of it.

examples.text:
